turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Dr. [Name]. Thank you for seeing me. So, honestly, what really made me finally pick up the phone and make this appointment—and I've been debating it for a few months now, probably ever since we shifted to this new quarterly planning model at my agency—is that I keep getting up during our long sales strategy meetings. 

I'm an advertising sales agent, and we have these massive, two- or three-hour meetings where we're going over ad buys and client pitches, and I know I’m supposed to just stay seated and take notes like everyone else. But I just... I can't seem to stay in my chair. I'll constantly find reasons to get up. I'll get up just to refill my water, even if my glass is practically full and I really don't need a drink, or I'll wander over and pace by the printer in the back of the conference room, acting like I'm waiting for a slide deck to print out when I'm really not. 

And the thing is, I know how it looks. The room is mostly glass, everyone else is perfectly planted in their ergonomic chairs, and I'm just popping up and down. My boss even gave me this look last Tuesday when I got up for the third time during the VP's presentation. It's just so frustrating because I know the expectation is to remain seated, but I just end up making excuses to pace around the back of the room anyway, and I feel like it's starting to become a whole thing at work.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient explicitly states they cannot stay in their chair and frequently get up to pace or refill water during long meetings where they are expected to remain seated.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of these work meetings, do you find yourself having similar difficulties sitting still in other situations—like during meals at home, watching TV, or in social gatherings?
turns.patient_response:
You know, it's funny you ask that, because I was actually just thinking about this the other day. I don't really have that problem at all outside of work. Like, if I'm at home? I can sit there for literally hours. Just this past Sunday, my boyfriend and I binge-watched almost an entire season of this new true-crime documentary on Netflix, and I was just totally glued to the sofa. I had my blanket, my snacks, and I didn't even want to get up to go to the kitchen. I just sat there the whole afternoon, completely fine. 

And with meals, it's the same thing. We usually eat on the couch, honestly, but even when we do sit at the actual dining table—like he made this really elaborate baked ziti a couple of nights ago, so we sat at the table to make it a nice dinner—I didn't feel that antsy, crawling-out-of-my-skin feeling at all. We just sat and ate and talked for probably an hour, and I didn't once feel the urge to jump up and check the mail or anything. 

Even in social situations, like if I'm out with my girlfriends... we have this spot downtown where we always get a corner booth, and we'll be there for three hours just catching up and having drinks, and I'm perfectly happy just staying put in the booth. I never feel like I need to go pace by the bathrooms or make up an excuse to stand. 

So, no, I really haven't noticed it outside of the office. It's so weird, right? It really just seems to be those specific, long, quiet conference room situations where I'm supposed to be a captive audience and look professional. When it's my own time, or I'm just relaxing or hanging out, I don't have that problem at all. I can just chill. It's just... I don't know, maybe it's the fluorescent lights at the agency or the pressure of the VP being right there, but yeah, at home or out and about, I'm totally fine sitting still.

symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient acknowledges that their need to stand or pace is isolated to 'specific, long, quiet conference room situations' at work.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient refers to an 'antsy, crawling-out-of-my-skin feeling' that they experience at work, confirming internal restlessness.
symptom_reasoning.S013: The patient explicitly denies difficulty relaxing during leisure time, stating they can 'just chill' and sit for hours watching TV or hanging out with friends.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient denies being constantly on the go, noting they can be 'glued to the sofa' for an entire afternoon without wanting to get up.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting in these long meetings and feeling the urge to get up, are you finding it hard to concentrate on what's being said, or is it more that you're feeling anxious or stressed about the meeting situation itself?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's definitely the concentration thing. I mean, I don't feel anxious or stressed about the meetings themselves, really. I know my accounts, I know the clients, so it's not like I'm sitting there terrified they're going to call on me and I won't know the answer. It's more like... okay, so we have these really long strategy meetings, right? And they always put up these massive PowerPoint decks. They're just so dense, with all these charts and projections. 

I'll sit down, and I'll have my notebook open, and I'll tell myself, 'Okay, this is the Q3 planning meeting, you need to pay attention, this is important.' And I really do start out focused. I'll listen to the first few minutes, maybe jot down a note about a new ad buy or something. But then... I don't know, it's like my brain just sort of unplugs? It happens when I'm reading client briefs at my desk, too. I'll be reading this three-page brief about a new campaign for a local car dealership, and I'll read the first paragraph, and I'm totally with it. But then, suddenly, five or ten minutes have gone by, and I realize I've just been staring at the exact same slide on the projector, or the exact same paragraph on my screen, and I have absolutely no idea what the last point was. 

It's like I'm physically looking at the words, but they aren't going into my brain. The VP will be talking about, I don't know, demographic targeting in the tri-state area, and I'll hear the sound of his voice, but I'm not actually processing a single thing he's saying. And then I have to frantically try to figure out where we are in the deck, or I have to reread the same paragraph in the brief like three or four times just to make it stick. That's usually when I start feeling like I need to get up and walk around, because I'm just sitting there, totally checked out, realizing I've completely lost the thread of the meeting again. It's so frustrating because I really am trying to pay attention, I just... I can't seem to hold onto it for more than a few minutes before I just drift off into space.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to maintain focus during long meetings and when reading briefs, losing the thread after just a few minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient mentions feeling the urge to get up and walk around when they lose focus during meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S059: The patient explicitly confirms having a 'concentration thing' where their brain 'unplugs' and they drift off into space.
symptom_reasoning.S056: The patient explicitly denies feeling anxious or stressed about the meetings.

turns.doctor_question: Going back to when you were in school—elementary, middle, high school—did you have similar difficulties concentrating or staying focused on lessons and assignments back then, or is this something that's more of a recent problem that started around the time of the new quarterly planning model at work?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, gosh, no, it's definitely not just a recent thing with the new planning model. I mean, the planning model just brought it out in a way that affects my job, but if I really think back... I remember this starting way, way before high school. Like, elementary school. 

My mom actually kept all my old report cards in this big plastic bin in the attic, and we were looking through them a couple of years ago when she moved, and it was honestly kind of eye-opening. Because every single teacher, from like second grade all the way up, wrote the exact same things in the comments section. They would always say I was a really bright kid, which, you know, is nice, but then there was always a catch. My elementary school teachers wrote that I was bright but I rushed through my work, or that I talked out of turn constantly. I was always interrupting people or just blurting things out because I felt like if I didn't say it right that second, my thought would just completely vanish. 

And the homework... oh my gosh, the homework. I would forget it all the time. I'd either forget to write down what the assignment was, or I'd actually do it at home and then just completely forget to turn it in the next morning. My desk was an absolute disaster zone, too. I remember my fourth-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable, she actually made me stay in during recess once just to clean it out, because it was literally stuffed to the brim with all these crumpled, half-finished papers and old worksheets that I just shoved in there instead of putting them away in my folders. 

So, yeah, it is definitely not new. It is like I have always been this way, just sort of scattered and leaving a trail of unfinished stuff, and I guess I just figured out how to handle it better or hide it better when I got to college and started working, right up until these massive three-hour agency meetings started and I couldn't just skate by on my own schedule anymore...

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient confirms the doctor's premise that their difficulties concentrating and staying focused on lessons have been present since elementary school.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes a history of failing to finish schoolwork, noting they left a trail of unfinished stuff and had a desk full of half-finished papers.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient states their desk was an absolute disaster zone because they shoved crumpled papers into it instead of organizing them into folders.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient reports constantly forgetting to write down homework assignments or forgetting to turn them in the next morning.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly mentions constantly blurting things out because they felt their thoughts would vanish if they didn't speak immediately.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient recalls that they were always interrupting people during their school years.

turns.doctor_question: When you were younger and had those thoughts that felt like they would disappear if you didn't say them right away—the ones where you'd blurt things out in class—do you still experience that same feeling now as an adult, where you feel like you have to act on something immediately or the urge will go away?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... no, actually. I don't think I really do that anymore. I mean, I think I kind of grew out of that specific thing? Or maybe adult life is just set up differently, you know? Like, back in elementary school, you're sitting there at your little desk and the teacher is at the chalkboard, and if you don't raise your hand right that exact second, the moment is completely gone and the class moves on to math or whatever. But now, working at the agency... well, first of all, if I just blurted things out during a pitch with a major client, my VP would probably have a literal heart attack right there in the conference room. So I definitely learned not to do that! 

And I don't really get that panicked, bubbling-up feeling of, like, 'I have to say this right this second or it's gone forever' anymore. If I have an idea for a campaign, or a question about a media buy while someone is talking, I just... I don't know, I'll jot it down on a sticky note. My desk is literally covered in those little neon pink and yellow Post-its for that exact reason. Or, honestly, I'll just shoot my coworker a Slack message. Slack is like a lifesaver for that, right? Because you can just type the thought the very second it pops into your head without actually interrupting anyone's sentence or derailing the whole meeting. 

So, yeah, I haven't really noticed that being a problem now. I mean, I talk a lot, obviously—my boyfriend always jokes that I could talk to a brick wall and get it to buy ad space—but I don't get that impulsive, desperate urge to just spit words out before they vanish like I did when I was a kid. I feel like I have a pretty good filter now, or at least I just know how to hold onto a thought, or write it down, until it's actually my turn to speak.

symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient explicitly states that she talks a lot and notes her boyfriend jokes she could talk to a brick wall.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient denies having the impulsive urge to spit words out or blurt things out like she did when she was a kid.
symptom_reasoning.S017: The patient states she knows how to hold onto a thought and wait until it is actually her turn to speak.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient mentions using alternative methods like Slack specifically to avoid interrupting anyone's sentence or derailing meetings.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned your desk is covered in Post-it notes now—how organized do you feel your work is overall? Do you find yourself struggling to keep track of deadlines, emails, or projects, or does the Post-it system actually work pretty well for you?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, the Post-its... well, I mean, they work for getting the thought out of my head in that exact second, like I was saying, but as an actual organizational system? It's... it's kind of a disaster, honestly. I try so hard to be organized, I really do. Every January, I go out and buy one of those really expensive, fancy leather-bound planners—you know the ones, where they have the hourly breakdowns and the little inspirational quotes at the top of every page, and the different colored ribbons to mark your place? I always tell myself, 'Okay, this is the year I'm going to have it all together, everything goes in the planner.' 

But then reality hits, and things get busy. I'll be on a call with a client—like last week, I was talking to the marketing director for this regional grocery chain we represent, and they were changing their whole Q4 strategy—and I'll just frantically scribble a note on a pink sticky note because it's right there. But then later, I'll be on my phone on the train and I'll email myself a reminder about their ad spend. And then I'll get to my desk and open a tab in Chrome with their competitor's pricing, and I just leave the tab open... I have like, I don't know, eighty tabs open across three different browser windows right now. 

So when it actually comes time to sit down and build the campaign strategy or put together the pitch deck, my notes are just completely scattered everywhere. They end up split between my emails, the sticky notes plastered all over my monitor, that expensive planner which I only half-use, and all those random browser tabs. It's just a total mess. And because it's so fragmented, I end up wasting just a ridiculous amount of time trying to piece it all back together. I'll sit there at my desk for forty-five minutes or an hour just staring at everything, trying to figure out what I'm supposed to do first, or which note is the most urgent, instead of just starting the actual work. 

It's like I have to go on a scavenger hunt through my own workspace before I can even begin to do my job. My boyfriend is always telling me I should just use Trello or Asana or one of those project management apps, because that's what his tech company uses, but I feel like if I try to learn a new digital system, I'll just end up with notes in Trello and on the sticky notes and in my email, you know? It wouldn't actually fix the problem, it would just add another place for me to lose my thoughts. So, yeah, I definitely wouldn't say I feel organized overall. It's more like controlled chaos, except half the time I'm not even the one controlling it.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states that their organizational system is a 'disaster,' their notes are scattered across multiple mediums, and they waste significant time trying to figure out what to do first instead of working.

turns.doctor_question: When you're out with your girlfriends or in social situations now, do you find yourself interrupting people while they're talking, or do you tend to blurt things out without thinking first?
turns.patient_response:
With my girlfriends? You know, actually, not so much. I mean, when we get together for drinks or brunch or whatever on the weekends, we all kind of just naturally talk over each other anyway. It's just a big, loud group of women catching up, so it’s hard to tell what’s actually interrupting and what’s just normal conversation for us, you know? 

But... oh, gosh, now that you ask it that way, I do actually do this at work. Like, a lot. It’s not exactly the same panicked feeling as when I was a kid blurting things out in class, but if I’m walking through the office and I suddenly think of an idea... like, say someone else is at their desk working through a pitch deck, or even if a couple of my coworkers are just having a conversation by the printer about a totally different account, I will literally just pop over and interrupt them to add my thought. I just barge right in! 

And it’s so frustrating because, almost the exact second after the words leave my mouth, I realize that it absolutely could have waited. Like, it wasn't an emergency, the client wasn't on fire, they were just trying to format a slide or talk about a media buy, and I just completely derailed their whole train of thought. I don't know why I do it. It's like, if I physically see the deck on their monitor, or I hear a keyword in their conversation, the idea just jumps out of my mouth before my brain can remind me to just go back to my desk and write it on one of my Post-its. My coworkers are usually pretty polite about it, but I always walk away kicking myself because I know I just interrupted their workflow for something that could have easily been an email two hours later. So, yeah, socially it doesn't stand out to me, but in the office I definitely still have that habit of just jumping in when it's really not necessary.

symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly confirms that she frequently interrupts her coworkers' conversations and workflows to share her thoughts, describing how she will 'barge right in' and jump in when it's not necessary.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned you interrupt your coworkers at work pretty regularly—do you also find yourself fidgeting, tapping your foot, or feeling restless in situations where you're supposed to be still, beyond just those long conference room meetings? Like at your desk while working, or even at home?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, um... fidgeting? No, actually, not really. I mean, I know some people are constant leg-bouncers or pen-clickers—like the guy in the cubicle next to me, Dave, he clicks his pen literally all day long and it drives me absolutely insane when I'm trying to concentrate—but I don't really do anything like that. When I'm at my desk, I'm actually pretty stationary. My agency actually just upgraded all our office furniture last year and got us these ridiculously expensive ergonomic chairs, the ones with the mesh backs and the lumbar support that you can adjust in like ten different ways? It took me like three days just to figure out all the levers and knobs on that thing. But anyway, once I get settled into it and I'm looking at my screens—I have a dual monitor setup plus my laptop, so it's a lot of screen real estate—I kind of just lock in. I don't really feel the need to squirm around or tap my feet or anything. If anything, I probably sit *too* still, because my Apple Watch is always buzzing at me at ten minutes to the hour telling me it's time to stand, and I'm always just swiping it away and ignoring it because I'm deep into an email thread or trying to fix the formatting on a pitch deck. 

And then at home... oh gosh, no, I'm definitely not restless at home. By the time I commute back to the apartment, which is a whole ordeal on the train especially with the recent track delays, I am completely exhausted. The absolute last thing I want to do is move around. My boyfriend and I have this massive, oversized sectional sofa that we bought from West Elm when we moved in together—it was our big splurge item, honestly way more than we should have spent, but it's so incredibly comfortable—and the second I get home, I change into my sweatpants and I just melt right into that couch corner. We'll put on whatever show we're currently binge-watching, right now it's that new cooking competition show, and I will literally just lay there like a log for three hours straight without moving a muscle. 

So, yeah, I don't get that physical restlessness at all. My brain might be going a million miles an hour with all those tabs open like I mentioned before, and I obviously have the issue with blurting things out at work, but physically? No, I'm pretty much planted exactly where I am. I don't get that urge to just get up and pace or bounce my leg. I'm actually perfectly happy just sitting still.

symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly acknowledges having an issue with blurting things out at work.
symptom_reasoning.S038: The patient describes their brain as 'going a million miles an hour with all those tabs open', indicating racing thoughts.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies fidgeting, squirming, or tapping their feet.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient denies the urge to get up and pace, stating they remain planted in their seat.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly denies experiencing physical restlessness, noting they are perfectly happy sitting still.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: When you're working at your desk on those client briefs or pitch decks that you mentioned earlier—the ones where you have to read through three pages or more—how often do you find yourself losing focus the way you described in the meetings, where you read something but don't actually process it, or do you find you can actually concentrate on your work when you're at your desk?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, it definitely happens at my desk, too. Honestly, it might even be worse when I'm just sitting there reading by myself. Because, you know, these client briefs we get—especially from the bigger corporate accounts, like that grocery chain I was talking about—they are just so incredibly dense. They'll send over these five or six-page PDFs of pure text, single-spaced, just going on and on about target demographics and Q4 KPIs and market penetration. 

I'll sit down in my fancy chair, and I'll tell myself, 'Okay, I'm going to read this whole thing right now and pull out the key metrics for the pitch.' And I really do start out focused! I'll have my yellow highlighter out, I'm sitting up straight, I'm ready to go. But then... I don't know, maybe three or four minutes in, I'll suddenly snap back to reality and realize I've just been staring at the exact same paragraph for who knows how long. My eyes will have physically moved over the words, but my brain is just... completely somewhere else. I'll get to the bottom of the page and realize I have absolutely zero idea what the last point even was. None. It's just blank. 

And it's not just when I'm reading briefs at my desk, either, it's the exact same thing in those longer strategy meetings. Like, we have these big all-hands meetings on Tuesday mornings where the VP goes over the quarterly projections, and there's always this massive, text-heavy PowerPoint. I'll be looking right at the screen, right at the presentation, nodding along like I'm totally engaged, and then I'll realize I've been staring at the exact same slide for five minutes and haven't absorbed a single word the presenter actually said. 

It's so frustrating because then I have to go back and re-read the brief from the very beginning, or I have to subtly message a coworker on Slack after the meeting to ask what we just agreed to, which makes me look like I don't care about the work. But I do care! I really do. It's just that my brain just kind of unplugs itself right in the middle of a sentence without my permission, and suddenly I'm just staring at a wall of text that means absolutely nothing to me.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly describes an inability to maintain focus during tasks like reading client briefs or attending strategy meetings, noting that their brain 'unplugs itself' and they fail to absorb the information after a few minutes.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features

turns.doctor_question: When you're doing something at work that you find genuinely interesting or engaging—like working on a pitch for a client you really like, or a campaign that excites you—do you still have that same problem where your mind goes blank and you lose focus, or is it mainly just with the dense, dry briefs and long strategy meetings?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, if it's something I actually find interesting? That's a completely different story. Like, a couple of months ago we were pitching this really cool indie cosmetics brand—they were doing this whole retro nineties grunge revival line, which is totally my aesthetic, by the way, I loved it—and I was just so incredibly into it. I could sit there for hours pulling mood boards, looking at competitor ads on Instagram, brainstorming taglines with the creative team, and I wouldn't even notice the time passing. My coffee would get completely cold on my desk because I was just so in the zone, you know? 

But then, if you switch gears and put me back in one of those longer strategy meetings, or hand me a client brief for something super dry like a B2B software company or that grocery chain I mentioned... it's exactly what I was just telling you. I'll go in with the absolute best intentions, I really do. I'll sit down, I'll start out totally focused, telling myself, 'Okay, let's nail down these deliverables, let's get this done.' But then, literally just a few minutes later, I'll catch myself. I'll suddenly realize I've been staring at the exact same slide on the projector, or the exact same paragraph in the PDF, and I have absolutely no idea what the last point was. 

It's like my brain just completely refuses to hold onto the information if it isn't sparkling and exciting. And I mean, I know I'm a professional, right? I'm thirty years old, I have a quota to meet, and I know I have to do the boring parts of the job too. You can't just only work on the fun makeup campaigns! Which is why it's so incredibly frustrating when I catch myself doing it. I'll just be sitting there, staring blankly at the same block of text, and I have to basically shake my head and force myself to start reading from the top of the page all over again. So, yeah, if it's a campaign that excites me, I'm totally fine, but the second it's one of those dense briefs or a long meeting, my brain just checks out after three minutes no matter how hard I try to pay attention.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly describes an inability to sustain attention during long meetings or when reading dry briefs, noting that their brain 'checks out after three minutes' despite their best efforts to focus.

top_partial.disease_name: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features
